fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. The verse says, “The idols of Egypt will tremble before Him…” Think about that for a second. Idols, and they're the ones shaking. The LORD shows up on a swift cloud and the idols tremble before Him.
Hiding is a good guess, and I know a little something about hiding. But the verse never says anything about hiding. It says the idols of Egypt will tremble before Him. That's the whole picture.
Melt is the word, baker. The verse says the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them. That's fear. I'd rather be a chocolate chip in a warm oven than a heart doing that.

Right, baker. The LORD says they will “…resort to idols and spirits of the dead, to mediums and spiritists.” (Isaiah 19:3) Their plans are frustrated, so that's where they turn. The verse lists it out: idols, spirits of the dead, mediums and spiritists.

Good thinking, but the verse never mentions Jerusalem or its priests. The text says they will resort to idols and spirits of the dead, to mediums and spiritists. That's who they turn to when their plans are frustrated.

Patient masters are the kind everybody hopes for, baker. But this verse says the Egyptians are delivered into the hands of a harsh master. The next line adds a fierce king who will rule over them. Patient isn't the word the text uses.

You got it, baker. The verse says, “The waters of the Nile will dry up, and the riverbed will be parched and empty.” Those are plain words for a river that has lost its water. The next verses go on to say the canals will stink and the reeds and rushes will wither.
A flood is the opposite problem, baker. This verse says the waters of the Nile will dry up. The riverbed ends up parched and empty, and verse 6 says the streams of Egypt will trickle and dry up.

That's right, it's false. Verse 8 says the fishermen will mourn, all who cast a hook into the Nile will lament, and those who spread nets on the waters will pine away. Mourning, lamenting and pining away are the opposite of celebrating. Sad folks, not party folks.

Assyria does show up near the end of this passage (Isaiah 19:23), but it isn't the one pouring here, baker. The verse says, “The LORD has poured into her a spirit of confusion.” The text names the LORD as the one who poured it.

It's the other way around, baker. Verse 21 says, “The LORD will make Himself known to Egypt, and on that day Egypt will acknowledge the LORD.” So Egypt doesn't refuse Him. The text says they will worship with sacrifices and offerings, and make vows to the LORD and fulfill them. Quite a turn from all the trembling earlier.

Worship is right, baker. The verse says, “The Egyptians and Assyrians will worship together.” Just before that, the text says there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, with the Assyrians going to Egypt and the Egyptians to Assyria. Two groups worshiping side by side is a picture worth looking at twice.

Fighting is a fair guess, friend. But verse 23 says the Egyptians and Assyrians will worship together. The highway between them has the Assyrians going to Egypt and the Egyptians to Assyria. The text names worship, not fighting.

Enemies isn't the word here, friend. The LORD of Hosts blesses them, saying, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.” Egypt is called His people, and Assyria is called His handiwork. Those are words for His own.

Israel is in the blessing, baker, and it's called His inheritance. The LORD says, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.” Egypt and Assyria are called His people and His handiwork. The blessing doesn't call either of them Israel's servants.
